chunks: Gain-bandwidth product. The question: What is the gain-bandwidth product?
The gain-bandwidth product (GBW) is a single number that says how much gain an op-amp (a standard amplifier chip) can give at what frequency.
Gain means how many times bigger the output is than the input. For most op-amps, gain times bandwidth stays constant.
So if you ask for more gain, you get less bandwidth, and the other way around.
Picture a fixed amount of paint. You can spread it thick over a small wall or thin over a large wall, but the total stays the same.
Gain is the thickness and bandwidth is the area. The analogy holds along the sloped part of the op-amp's gain curve.
It does not describe very low frequencies, down to steady (DC) signals, where the gain is flat.
Open-loop gain (top curve) is flat at 100 decibels until 10 hertz, then falls 20 decibels/decade, hitting 0 decibels at 1 megahertz.
Closing the loop for a gain of 10 (20 decibels) flattens the response up to about 100 kilohertz, where it meets the open-loop line. Gain 100 (40 decibels) gives 10 kilohertz.
All the curves share the same roll-off line: gain times bandwidth is constant. Drag GBW: every closed-loop corner slides with it.
Drag G₂ toward 1000: its flat region shrinks in exact proportion, but it still meets the same open-loop line.
Open-loop gain: the op-amp's raw gain with no feedback. Closed-loop gain: the gain set by the feedback network. Bandwidth: the range of frequencies the amplifier handles well.
Dominant pole: the low frequency where the gain starts to fall. Unity-gain frequency: where the gain drops to 1. It equals the GBW.
Take an op-amp with a 1 megahertz GBW. Set up a gain of 10, and the bandwidth is about 1 megahertz over 10 equals 100 kilohertz.
Set up a gain of 100, and the bandwidth is about 10 kilohertz. A gain of 1 has about 1 megahertz.
Pick the op-amp by multiplying the gain you need by the highest frequency you need, then add margin. That is the whole idea.
"The gain-bandwidth product is the constant you get by multiplying gain by frequency along the amplifier's roll-off.
A voltage-feedback op-amp has a huge DC gain with a dominant pole at a low frequency, then falls 20 decibels per decade, so gain times frequency is constant and equals the unity-gain frequency.
With feedback, closed-loop bandwidth is the GBW divided by the closed-loop noise gain, so a 1 megahertz op-amp running at a gain of 10 gives about 100 kilohertz.
I use it to pick an op-amp: the gain I need times the highest signal frequency, with margin."
